text: Lara Croft is the main protagonist of the Tomb Raider video game franchise, created by Core Design, a British developer led by Toby Gard, who first appeared in the 1996 game Tomb Raider. Gard designed her as a counter to stereotypical female characters, inspired by icons like Neneh Cherry and Tank Girl, and initially envisioned a male lead before settling on a female character after observing player preferences in Virtua Fighter. He aimed for realism in animation and avoided clichéd portrayals, such as "bimbos" or "dominatrix" types, and cited a desire to create a relatable, enigmatic, and strong female figure. The character's name was changed from Laura Cruz to Lara Croft, with "Lara" chosen for its Greek roots meaning "citadel" and "Croft" derived from a Derby phonebook. Her original backstory described her as the daughter of Lord Henshingly Croft, raised as a British aristocrat, attending Gordonstoun and a Swiss finishing school, and surviving a plane crash in the Himalayas at age 21, which led her to pursue adventure and publish works as a mercenary and thief. In the second era beginning with Tomb Raider: Legend (2006), her origin was revised: she is the daughter of archaeologist Lord Richard Croft, Earl of Abingdon, and after a plane crash at age nine with her mother Amelia, who vanishes after tampering with an ancient sword, she becomes determined to uncover the truth. In the third era, starting with Tomb Raider (2013), Lara traveled with her parents on archaeological expeditions, where her mother disappeared and her father presumably died, leaving her in the care of Conrad Roth; she studied at University College London instead of Cambridge, met her friend Samantha Nishimura, and later joined an expedition to the Dragon's Triangle in search of the lost civilization of Yamatai, where she developed into a survivor through supernatural experiences. Core Design developed Lara's character over time, increasing the polygon count of her 3D model from 230 in the first game to 300 in Tomb Raider III, and later to 4,400 in The Angel of Darkness, and eventually over 9,800 and 32,000 in later titles. The character's appearance evolved with new outfits, such as a V-neck crop top, camouflage pants, and black or light brown shorts, and her hairstyle changed from a braid to a ponytail. Her accessories include fingerless gloves, a backpack, a utility belt with holsters, and two pistols, with gameplay adding abilities like swimming, crawling, and melee attacks. The character's voice was voiced by Shelley Blond initially, then Judith Gibbins, and later Keeley Hawes. Crystal Dynamics, which took over after the 2003 game Tomb Raider: The Angel of Darkness was poorly received, rebooted the franchise by focusing on believability, emotional depth, and realistic movement, using motion capture with stuntwoman Heidi Moneymaker, and introducing real-time environmental effects like wet skin and dirt accumulation. The developers emphasized fluid animations, emotional responses, and realistic proportions, reducing breast size and increasing body muscle tone. Lara Croft holds six Guinness World Records, has a strong fan following, and is among the first video game characters to be successfully adapted to film. She is considered a sex symbol and a significant figure in popular culture, though her influence has sparked debate among critics as both a positive change in video games and a controversial role model for young girls. The character has appeared in video games, printed media, animated shorts, films, and merchandise, including apparel, accessories, action figures, and third-party promotions in television, print, music, and advertising. Square Enix acquired Eidos in April 2009, restructuring it into Square Enix Europe, but Crystal Dynamics continued as the developer of the Tomb Raider series.

Lara Croft is the protagonist of the Tomb Raider video game series, published by Square Enix Europe (formerly Eidos Interactive), where she travels the world in search of rare objects and mystical artefacts. She first appeared in the 1996 game Tomb Raider, competing against a rival archaeologist for an Atlantean artefact, followed by Tomb Raider II (1997) focusing on the Dagger of Xian, Tomb Raider III (1998) involving meteorite fragments that grant supernatural powers, and Tomb Raider: The Last Revelation (1999), which features a young Croft accompanied by her mentor Werner Von Croy as she searches for artefacts linked to the Egyptian god Horus. Tomb Raider: Chronicles (2000) uses flashbacks to tell its story, while portable titles include Tomb Raider (2000) on Game Boy Color, seeking the Nightmare Stone, Tomb Raider: Curse of the Sword (2001) against a cult, and Tomb Raider: The Prophecy (2002) on Game Boy Advance centered on three magical stones. Tomb Raider: The Angel of Darkness (2003) centers on the murder of Professor Von Croy. Eidos rebooted the series with Tomb Raider: Legend (2006), altering Croft’s backstory as she searches for Excalibur and her mother, and Tomb Raider: Anniversary (2007) remade the first game with design elements from Legend. Tomb Raider: Underworld (2008) continues the plot, focusing on Croft’s search for information about her mother’s disappearance and the existence of Thor’s hammer, Mjölnir. Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light (2010) introduces cooperative gameplay set in a Central American jungle, featuring an ancient warrior, and uses the same technology as previous Tomb Raider games. In 2013, the series was rebooted with a new game that retold Lara’s origins, beginning a new continuity, followed by Rise of the Tomb Raider (2015) and Shadow of the Tomb Raider (2018). Crystal Dynamics aimed to make the character more human and relatable, addressing her "Teflon coating" by creating a more grounded, empathetic version with realistic proportions, a ponytail, "M-shaped" lips, and specific facial features, and designed functional, youthful, and practical outfits. Eye tracking studies were conducted to evaluate the redesign. The studio introduced new combat mechanics, including a free aiming system to foster a "raw, brutal, and desperate" style, reflecting Lara’s inexperience with violence and her traumatic first act of killing. The new Tomb Raider features motion capture-based animation with face and voice performances to enhance realism and emotion. Crystal Dynamics sought to make the visual appearance of the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 versions identical, using different techniques on each system. In response to Underworld's poor sales, Eidos reportedly considered altering Lara’s appearance to appeal more to female fans. The 2018 film Tomb Raider, directed by Roar Uthaug, draws inspiration from the 2013 reboot and features Angelina Jolie reprising her role in the 2001 film and the 2003 sequel, The Cradle of Life. Jolie trained rigorously for stunts, used minimal padding to achieve a 36D bust, and avoided showing unrealistic video game proportions to young girls. Outside the games, Lara Croft appears in Brawlhalla as a Diana DLC skin, in Astro's Playroom, in Fortnite Battle Royale’s sixth season and a "Team Up!" mode with Aloy from Horizon Zero Dawn, in a 2025 Angel of Darkness-styled skin, and in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare II’s Season 5 Reloaded. She is also a playable character in Hero Wars: Alliance and Hero Wars: Dominion Era during a time-limited event and a playable survivor in Dead by Daylight’s Tomb Raider DLC, released on 16 July 2024. The character has appeared in comics by Top Cow Productions, starting with a crossover in Witchblade and a solo series from 1999, with stories unrelated to games until issue 32, which adapted Angel of Darkness. Additional novels include The Amulet of Power (2003), The Lost Cult (2004), and The Man of Bronze (2005). GameTap released Revisioned: Tomb Raider in 2007, a web series of ten animated films with re-imagined versions of Croft by artists like Jim Lee and Warren Ellis, featuring Minnie Driver as the character. Hayley Atwell voices Lara in the Netflix animated series Tomb Raider: The Legend of Lara Croft. Eidos’s German branch and KMF agency handled marketing, with no focus groups or scientific studies consulted, and marketing efforts emphasized attractiveness while avoiding excessive clothing in European press, and Eidos declined most merchandising proposals, focusing on game development. After Square Enix acquired Eidos in April 2009, marketing duties were transferred to Square Enix Europe, and the second reboot aligned all products and promotions with the new character version. Lara Croft has appeared on the cover of numerous video game and non-video game publications, including The Face, Time, Newsweek, Focus, and the Financial Times, with over 2,300 cover appearances by April 2025, earning a Guinness World Record. Eidos licensed the character for advertisements, including for Visa, Lucozade, G4 TV, Brigitte, and SEAT cars, and used her in a commercial for Gordonstoun boarding school due to Core Design’s inclusion of the school in the game’s biography. She became a spokesmodel for the Skin Cancer Awareness Foundation in 2006. Merchandise includes action figures by Toy Biz and Playmates Toys, 1/6-scale model kits by Marc Klinnert, life-size statues promoted by arcade and PlayStation magazines, autographed cards due to fan demand, themed wallpapers and Xbox 360 avatars, apparel like wallets, watches, bathrobes, and Zippo lighters, hiking boots, backpacks, leather jackets, and thermoses, and appearances on French postage stamps, PlayStation memory cards, and trading cards. In 1997, Eidos held an art exhibition titled "Lara Goes Art" in Hamburg, featuring fan and artist submissions including oil paintings, photo comics, and computer-generated footage. Eidos hired models to portray Lara at events and promotions.

Eidos released a brand of Lara Croft apparel and accessories under the label "LARA," including wallets, watches, bathrobes, and Zippo lighters. Third-party apparel such as hiking boots, backpacks, leather jackets, and thermoses also features Croft's likeness. Her image has appeared on French postage stamps, PlayStation memory cards, and trading cards as part of a collectible card game. In October 1997, Eidos held an art exhibition titled "Lara Goes Art" in Hamburg, Germany to promote Tomb Raider II, featuring oil and airbrushed paintings, photo comics, and Klinnert's model, with SZM Studios providing computer-generated footage for Die Ärzte's music video and the Brigitte magazine television commercial. Eidos hired several models to portray Lara Croft at publicity events, promotions, trade shows, and photo shoots. Initially, four models dressed as Lara for a photo call, but after drawing an unusually large crowd, Eidos expanded the concept by casting a single official Lara. Nathalie Cook portrayed the character from 1996 to 1997, followed by British actress Rhona Mitra from 1997 to 1998. Core Design restricted Mitra's dialogue, allowing only in-character answers if pre-reviewed and scripted. French model Vanessa Demouy succeeded Mitra briefly, before fashion model Nell McAndrew took over at the 1998 Electronic Entertainment Expo, selected from around 150 women who auditioned, including one with a shaved head. McAndrew portrayed Croft from 1998 to 1999 when Eidos fired her for posing in Playboy, which used the character and franchise without Eidos's approval; Core Design obtained an injunction against the magazine, requiring stickers on the cover to conceal the reference. Eidos later donated McAndrew's Tomb Raider costume to a UNICEF charity auction. Lara Weller followed from 1999 to 2000, Lucy Clarkson from 2000 to 2002, and Jill de Jong from 2002 to 2004, wearing a costume based on Lara Croft's appearance in Angel of Darkness. Karima Adebibe became the model from 2006 to 2008, the first allowed to portray Lara outside photography, and trained in combat, motorcycling, elocution, and conduct. Gymnast Alison Carroll succeeded her in 2008, wearing apparel based on the character's appearance in Underworld, and received special training in SAS survival, weapons, and archaeology. Crystal Dynamics discontinued the use of models as part of the franchise's second reboot. The number of models led Guinness World Records to award Lara Croft the official record for the "most official real life stand-ins" in 2008. Lara Croft's introduction was widely regarded as an innovation in the video game market, with Rob Smith of PlayStation: The Official Magazine calling her a video game icon of that generation. IGN credited a rise in PlayStation sales to her debut, and PlayStation Magazine attributed the first title's success to the character, with official U.S. PlayStation Magazine stating that Tomb Raider's success propelled her to prominence as a system mascot. PlayStation Magazine credited coverage in the Financial Times in 1997 as the starting point of her mainstream attention, noting that the newspaper featured Lara to illustrate Eidos's financial results, which Eidos had not actively promoted. As years progressed, Lara Croft's popularity declined due to poorly received sequels, with the Angel of Darkness often cited as her low point. IGN editor Colin Moriarty stated that she became more like a "virtual blow-up doll." Crystal Dynamics' rendition in Legend received wide, though not universal, praise, with Game Informer naming her the number six top video game hero of 2006, citing the successful reboot. Chris Slate of PlayStation Magazine praised the changes in Legend, calling Lara "finally back," highlighting new gameplay and appearance. Some critics, such as Schedeen and Patrick Shaw of GamePro, felt the makeover did not improve the character, and fans disapproved of the switch from the braid. Dr. Mark Griffiths of Nottingham Trent University described Lara Croft as a psychological tabula rasa, while Richard Rouse of Midway Games attributed her appeal to a loosely defined personality allowing players to project themselves onto her. Jeremy Smith stated that the minimal personality enables players to form a relationship with her, sharing the game experience rather than taking on the role. Burton noted that Croft is perceived differently around the world: French audiences focus on her sex appeal, while German and British audiences are drawn to her aggressiveness and aloofness. Fansites dedicated to Lara Croft appeared in several languages after the release of Tomb Raider, with over 100 by the end of 1998, and by 2000, HotBot yielded around 4,700 pages for a search of her name. Fans discussed rumors about her via usenet newsgroups and ICQ chats, collected merchandise, submitted fan art, participated in cosplay, and obtained tattoos. One admirer rode a bike over 500 miles (800 km) from Amsterdam to Derby wearing Lara Croft-brand clothing to meet developers, who welcomed him. Lara Croft holds a Guinness World Record as the "most recognized female video game character," received a star on the Walk of Game in San Francisco, and has been described by magazines as one of the iconic and best female video game characters of all time. Game Informer noted her popularity worldwide, especially in England, while official U.S. PlayStation Magazine described her as "one of today's premier videogame and movie heroes" and Play magazine as "3D gaming's first female superstar." Hartas called her one of the most famous game women, praising her independence. Karen Jones of Official U.S. PlayStation Magazine described her as "one of the biggest stars on the PlayStation." In 1998 and 2004, PlayStation Magazine called her one of the most memorable characters on the PlayStation console. Time magazine writer Chris Taylor called her "the foundation of one of the most successful franchises in video-game history." Guinness World Records named her the best-selling video game heroine in November 2025, following the Tomb Raider franchise surpassing 100 million units sold. Lara Croft has become a sex symbol for video games, despite Toby Gard's intention for her to be sexy "only because of her power." Time magazine's Kristina Dell considered her the first sex symbol of video games, and Schedeen stated she was among the first video game icons accepted as a mainstream sex symbol. Robert Ashley of Official U.S. PlayStation Magazine described her as the first video game character openly thought of as sexy, attributing the rise of similar 3D characters to her. Several publications listed big breasts as one of her most famous attributes. In 2008, she was first and second on two UGO Networks lists of hottest video game characters, and GameDaily placed her number one on a similar list. PlayStation: The Official Magazine awarded her honourable mention for Game Babe of the Year. She appeared in several issues of Play's Girls of Gaming and PlayStation Magazine's Swimsuit special, with layouts portraying her partially nude, in bikinis, and in revealing cocktail dresses, though Tomb Raider: Underworld's creative director Eric Lindstrom criticized such poses as out of character, stating they conflict with her strengths and that fans respond more strongly to conservative depictions. PlayStation Magazine staff agreed, noting that better use of her sex appeal would please fans. Male players have performed in-game actions to make Lara Croft say phrases and view closer camera angles of her bust, and pornography featuring her has been distributed online. After the first game's release, rumors appeared about a cheat code to remove her clothes, despite Core Design's denial, fueled by manipulated nude images. Eidos management viewed the rumor as good publicity and internally recommended including it in future game development. The rumor persisted through the release of Legend. PlayStation Magazine featured an April Fool's parody of Croft and the rumored code called "Nude Raider." Fans developed software patches to remove her clothing in personal computer game releases. Reactions from groups have been mixed; the journal Leonardo noted some feminists' negative reactions, with males identifying with their feminine side through Croft, reinforcing unrealistic ideals about the female body. Australian feminist scholar Germaine Greer criticized her as an embodiment of male fantasies. Electronic Gaming Monthly argued that Croft continued the trend of female characters being large-breasted and scantily clad to appeal to a predominantly male audience, teaching gamers to see women as sex objects. PlayStation Magazine staff noted that Croft could be seen as either a role model for young independent girls or a male adolescent fantasy, though they later stated she did little to attract female demographics and was designed for a male audience. The magazine also criticized Core Design's hypocrisy in downplaying her sex appeal while releasing advertisements that prominently featured it. Graphic artist Heather Gibson attributed the "sexism" to Eidos's marketing department. Author Mark Cohen attributed her eroticism among male fans to her appearance and a male protective instinct, with German psychologist Oscar Holzberg describing the behavior as stemming from the opportunity to act as a hero in virtual worlds and a fear of powerful, emancipated women. Jonathan Smith of Arcade: The Videogame Magazine noted that male players often see themselves as "chivalrous protectors." Holzberg further stated that the lower psychological investment in virtual characters is more comfortable for males. Cohen affirmed that despite her male appeal, Croft garnered a serious female audience, with Eidos estimating that by 2000 female consumers comprised 20–25 percent of Tomb Raider game purchases. Jeremy Smith argued that the series attracted more female players to video gaming, especially in Japan, and believed Croft does not alienate prospective female players, representing an emancipated heroine rather than just an attractive character. Adrian Smith noted her popularity with younger demographics that did not view her sexually. Cohen reasoned that Croft differs from other erotic characters because the Tomb Raider games feature rich action, impressive graphics, and intelligent puzzles, unlike other characters with lacking content. Amy Hennig of Naughty Dog and Griffiths echoed similar statements. GamesRadar editor Justin Towell nonetheless stated he couldn't imagine a Tomb Raider game without a sexualized female lead. Griffith described Lara Croft as a flawed female influence, stating that though she is a step in the right direction, many women view her as a "crudely realised male fantasy figure." Women in the video game industry describe her as both a positive and negative influence. Ismini Roby of WomenGamers.com stated that in 1996, Croft was not a sexist influence due to the lack of prominent female characters, and though her over-sexualized appearance was overlooked as a "breath of fresh air," she felt the character's personality was diluted by developer actions to appeal to a male audience. LesbianGamers.com's Tracy Whitelaw called her a dichotomy, stating that while she is viewed as "idealized" with an "unattainable body," she was a great stride for female characters as video game protagonists. Lara Croft's 1996 debut is often cited as a catalyst for more female leads in video games. Kaiser Hwang of PlayStation Magazine stated she "brought girl power" to video games. IGN argued that she helped redefine gender in video games by providing a different interpretation of what women could do. Several publications have used her as the standard for later female video game characters. Multiple video game publications have labeled her a video game and cultural icon. The title character in the 1998 German film Run Lola Run has often been compared to Croft. Comparisons were also made to Bond girl Christmas Jones from the 1999 James Bond film The World Is Not Enough. Eidos Interactive senior executive John Davis and character spokeswoman Susie Hamilton noted the character's similarities to Lara Croft. Jeremy Smith credits Croft with exposing the Tomb Raider games and video games in general to a wider audience. Computer and Video Games noted that her appearance on the cover of The Face signaled a change in the perception of video games from "geeky" to mainstream. The character is honored in the English city Derby, the former home of Core Design. In 2007, Radleigh Homes placed a blue plaque for Croft at the site of Core Design's former offices. In 2009, Derby City Council opened a public vote to name its new ring road, with "Lara Croft Way" winning by 89% of over 27,000 votes and opening in July 2010. In 2020, Croft appeared on four commemorative UK postage stamps issued by the Royal Mail to celebrate classic UK video games. A 2024 poll conducted by BAFTA with around 4,000 respondents named Lara Croft as the most iconic video-game character of all time. Yahoo! Movies and IGN credit Jolie.

Lara Croft's influence has expanded to a wider audience, with Computer and Video Games noting that Croft's appearance on the cover of The Face marked a shift in how video games were perceived, moving from "geeky" to mainstream.[11] In Derby, the English city formerly home to Core Design, Croft is honored through a blue plaque installed in 2007 by Radleigh Homes at the site of Core Design's former offices, now a block of flats.[225] In 2009, Derby City Council launched a public vote to name its new ring road, with "Lara Croft Way" winning by 89% of over 27,000 votes and officially opening in July 2010.[226][227][228] In 2020, Croft was featured on four commemorative UK postage stamps issued by the Royal Mail to celebrate classic UK video games.[229] A 2024 BAFTA poll with approximately 4,000 respondents named Lara Croft as the most iconic video-game character of all time.[230] Yahoo! Movies and IGN credited Angelina Jolie's role in the first Tomb Raider film with significantly raising her profile and propelling her to international super-stardom, respectively.[231][232] Jolie stated that young children would ask her to sign objects as Lara Croft.[95] After filming at the Cambodian temple Ta Prohm, locals referred to it as the "Angelina Jolie Temple" and local restaurants began serving Jolie's favorite alcoholic beverage as "Tomb Raider cocktails."[233] IGN's Jesse Schedeen described Croft as one of the few characters to receive a decent video game-to-movie adaptation.[162] By 2008, the first Tomb Raider film had become the highest-grossing video game film and the largest opening ever for a movie headlined by a woman.[31][234] It was the second highest-grossing video game movie in 2010, following the release of Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time,[235] with Lara Croft Tomb Raider: The Cradle of Life ranking as the fourth.[236]
